question: During which phase of a community diagnosis do nurses actually go out to collect field data?

options.A: Survey phase
options.B: Reporting phase
options.C: Evaluation phase
options.D: Pre-survey phase

explanation: You nailed it! The survey phase is the action time when nurses hit the field to gather data through interviews and observations.

question: Why is proper patient allocation so important during staffing?

options.A: It ensures everyone works the exact same night shifts
options.B: It eliminates the need for shift handovers
options.C: It matches staff skills and experience with patient care needs
options.D: It guarantees hospital operating costs stay at zero

explanation: Matching the right nurse to the right patient keeps everyone safe and prevents junior nurses from feeling overwhelmed.

question: Which serious complication of a peptic ulcer causes a hard, board-like abdomen and severe pain?

options.A: Pyloric stenosis
options.B: Perforation
options.C: Pernicious anemia
options.D: Gastric reflux

explanation: Spot on! If an ulcer burns right through the stomach wall, stomach contents leak into the belly, causing a medical emergency with a very rigid, painful abdomen.

question: Why should you check physical vital signs alongside what a patient tells you?

options.A: Verbal reports are completely useless in a clinical setting.
options.B: Vital signs are the only legal way to document emotional distress.
options.C: Patients always lie about how much pain they are feeling.
options.D: Physical signs can reveal high anxiety even if the patient claims to be fine.

explanation: You got it! A patient might try to act brave and say 'I'm okay,' but a racing pulse or high blood pressure can give away their true stress level.

question: Which of these is a classic example of a structural barrier to health behaviour change?

options.A: The specific age distribution of the community
options.B: Personal stubbornness of the local village chief
options.C: Poor road networks and lack of facility equipment
options.D: A patient's lack of interest in taking medications

explanation: Structural barriers are physical or infrastructural roadblocks—like bad roads or broken clinic gear—that make healthy choices harder to practice.

question: Why is community ownership so important for the long-term success of health projects?

options.A: It guarantees that the clinic will make a profit from drug sales.
options.B: It removes all responsibilities from the shoulders of community nurses.
options.C: Locals will sustain and protect the program after external support ends.
options.D: Government health budgets will no longer be needed at all.

explanation: Exactly! When the community feels the project is theirs, they will keep it running strong long after outsiders pack up and leave.

question: A patient is scheduled for an abdominal CT with IV contrast. What is the very first thing a nurse should check?

options.A: Administer a full dose of oral laxatives to clear the bowel
options.B: Assess the patient for a history of seafood or iodine allergies
options.C: Shave the hair on the patient's abdomen near the umbilicus
options.D: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter for continuous output

explanation: Safety first! Checking for allergies prevents severe reactions to the iodine contrast. You are thinking like a real nurse!

question: Which nerve supplies the main feeling and sensation to the external female genitalia?

options.A: The obturator nerve
options.B: The femoral nerve
options.C: The pudendal nerve
options.D: The sciatic nerve

explanation: Great recall! The pudendal nerve is the main pathway supplying feeling to the perineum and external genitalia.

question: Which hormone tells the bone marrow to make more red blood cells during pregnancy?

options.A: Oxytocin
options.B: Erythropoietin
options.C: Progesterone
options.D: Prolactin

explanation: Erythropoietin is like a special chemical messenger released by the kidneys to tell the bone marrow, 'Hey, we need more red blood cells for the baby!'

question: Why do we ask family planning clients to come back for follow-up visits?

options.A: To administer routine childhood immunizations
options.B: To conduct major diagnostic surgical procedures
options.C: To permanently discharge the client from care
options.D: To check on the client and offer ongoing support

explanation: Follow-up visits are all about seeing how the client is doing and giving them continuous support with their chosen contraceptive method.

question: What is the main goal of cancer rehabilitation?

options.A: Curing the primary cancer diagnosis
options.B: Preventing the recurrence of tumors
options.C: Managing acute surgical site infections
options.D: Restoring physical and emotional well-being

explanation: You got this! Cancer rehab is all about helping patients get back their strength, independence, and good quality of life after treatment.

question: In a formal research report, which section will you find the reliability scores of the measurement tools?

options.A: Acknowledgements
options.B: References
options.C: Methods
options.D: Introduction

explanation: The Methods section is the researcher's 'recipe book'—it's where they explain every tool used and how reliable it was.

question: What is the primary function of the sensory strip located in the parietal lobe?

options.A: Processing touch, pain, and temperature
options.B: Regulating heartbeat and breathing
options.C: Controlling voluntary muscle movement
options.D: Interpreting visual images and colors

explanation: The sensory strip receives incoming touch and temperature signals from different parts of the body. [learn more](GNS211_U3_T23#GNS211_U3_T23_h3)

question: What is the main responsibility of the supplementary motor area (SMA)?

options.A: Regulating baseline heart rate and breathing
options.B: Processing sharp pain and temperature sensations
options.C: Planning and sequencing complex movements
options.D: Translating spoken words into written text

explanation: You've got this! The SMA acts like a master planner, organizing movement sequences before you actually perform them.

question: Why do hospital disaster plans include steps for safely discharging stable patients?

options.A: To free up critical bed space and medical resources for incoming disaster casualties
options.B: To comply with international travel regulations for foreign medical volunteers
options.C: To punish patients who have overstayed their expected recovery duration
options.D: To reduce the hospital's monthly utility bills during a crisis event

explanation: When an emergency brings in dozens of critically injured people, sending home stable patients creates the vital bed space needed to save lives.

question: What is the radioactive tracer most commonly used in a PET scan?

options.A: Iodinated contrast
options.B: Gadolinium chelate
options.C: Fluorodeoxyglucose
options.D: Barium sulfate

explanation: Great job! Fluorodeoxyglucose (often called FDG) is a form of sugar attached to a tiny radioactive tag, making it the perfect tracer to see which cells are gobbling up energy.

question: Who is the main age group focused on in the IMNCI strategy?

options.A: Infants in their first year of life
options.B: School-age children up to twelve years
options.C: Toddlers between one and three years
options.D: Children under five years of age

explanation: The IMNCI guidelines are specially made to tackle the biggest health challenges and save the lives of children under five years old. Great job!

question: Which medication class is widely known to cause constipation as a side effect?

options.A: Short-acting diuretics
options.B: Opioid pain relievers
options.C: Inhaled bronchodilators
options.D: Broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Opioids slow down gastrointestinal motility significantly, which frequently leads to stubborn constipation in patients taking them. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T6#GNS212_U1_T6_h2)

question: What is the main thing that sets a community health nurse apart from a hospital ward nurse?

options.A: They go out into the community to assess and promote health
options.B: They never perform basic clinical procedures or wound care
options.C: They only prescribe medications without doctor supervision
options.D: They exclusively work inside large government laboratories

explanation: Instead of waiting inside hospital walls, community nurses step right out into the streets, homes, and schools to care for people.

question: How does the Drug Control Act directly affect daily nursing practice?

options.A: It decides which patients receive free medical care
options.B: It dictates the special handling rules for dangerous drugs
options.C: It sets the standard uniform code for hospital wards
options.D: It determines how many hours a nurse can work per week

explanation: The law sets clear rules on how nurses must store, give, and record potent medications. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T13#GNS122_U1_T13_h2)

question: What is the primary role of calcitriol, the active form of vitamin D produced by the kidneys?

options.A: Stimulating red blood cell maturation
options.B: Increasing systemic blood pressure
options.C: Regulating blood glucose concentrations
options.D: Promoting calcium absorption in the gut

explanation: Calcitriol helps maintain strong bones by ensuring adequate dietary calcium is absorbed from the intestines. [learn more](GNS121_U2_T1#GNS121_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why is it important to regularly calibrate hospital research equipment?

options.A: To prevent measurement errors that ruin data accuracy
options.B: To shorten the time required for patient interviews
options.C: To make the equipment look newer to inspectors
options.D: To ensure patients pay lower hospital bills

explanation: Exactly right! If our tools aren't accurate, our data won't be either. Calibration keeps our numbers honest.

question: What happens to the airways in your lungs when the sympathetic nervous system kicks in?

options.A: Complete airway closure
options.B: Bronchodilation
options.C: Bronchoconstriction
options.D: Increased mucus secretion

explanation: When you face stress or danger (fight or flight), your body opens up your airways wide so you can take in more oxygen quickly!

question: What is the main goal of workplace ergonomics in nursing?

options.A: Reducing the number of patients assigned to each nurse
options.B: Eliminating the need for taking breaks during a shift
options.C: Fitting the work environment and equipment to the worker
options.D: Speeding up the documentation process on computer terminals

explanation: Spot on! Ergonomics is all about shaping your tools and workspace to match your body, making your daily tasks safer and more comfortable. [learn more](GNS113_U3_T3#GNS113_U3_T3_h1)

question: What is the main goal of mitigation in disaster management?

options.A: To provide immediate medical care during a crisis
options.B: To reduce the severity of potential hazards
options.C: To conduct evacuation drills right before a storm
options.D: To rebuild homes after a disaster has occurred

explanation: Mitigation is all about taking action *before* a disaster strikes to lessen its blow on people and property. Think of it as putting up strong safeguards early! [learn more](GNS315_U1_T9#GNS315_U1_T9_h1)

question: What is the best long-term way to prevent ascariasis outbreaks in communities?

options.A: Administering yearly vaccinations to all newborns
options.B: Improving sanitation infrastructure and health education
options.C: Spraying chemical pesticides on all residential soil
options.D: Isolating infected individuals in quarantine wards

explanation: Stopping the cycle comes down to the basics: clean water, proper toilets, handwashing, and community health education.

question: Why is the final monitoring and evaluation step so important in the Nutrition Care Process?

options.A: To replace the initial nutrition diagnosis with a new disease
options.B: To bill the hospital insurance company for services rendered
options.C: To discharge the patient immediately from the hospital ward
options.D: To check if the nutritional plan is working and make changes

explanation: Correct! Monitoring lets us see if our dietary plan is actually helping the patient or if we need to switch things up.

question: Which items are absolute must-haves in a basic household emergency kit?

options.A: Portable safe water and non-perishable food
options.B: Large furniture pieces for protection
options.C: Board games and entertainment books
options.D: Expensive electronics and jewelry

explanation: Correct! Clean water and food are your top survival essentials when regular utilities and shops shut down during a disaster.

question: Which skin gland makes an oily substance called sebum to keep your hair and skin soft?

options.A: Ceruminous gland
options.B: Apocrine gland
options.C: Sebaceous gland
options.D: Eccrine gland

explanation: Correct! Sebaceous glands are our natural oil producers, keeping our skin waterproofed and conditioned.

question: What actually defines an ethical dilemma in nursing?

options.A: A situation where two or more moral principles conflict with each other
options.B: A disagreement between a nurse and a doctor over medication dosage
options.C: A patient refusing to pay their nursing agency bills
options.D: A broken piece of medical equipment inside the patient's home

explanation: Spot on! It's a tough spot where every choice seems to break a moral rule, and there is no easy right or wrong answer.

question: Why is noting the exact time of death so crucial for the healthcare team?

options.A: It determines how long the bed stays empty
options.B: It dictates the cost of the hospital bill
options.C: It starts legal and administrative timelines
options.D: It proves the nurse followed hospital policy

explanation: Spot on! The recorded time marks the official start for all the legal paperwork, death certificates, and hospital records that follow.

question: What is a common challenge that QA committees face in many Nigerian hospitals?

options.A: Excessive funding that makes budget management difficult
options.B: Too much free time for clinical staff during working hours
options.C: Having way too many medical doctors and nurses in every ward
options.D: Severe staff shortages and heavy workloads leading to fatigue

explanation: True indeed! Manpower shortages and burnout are everyday hurdles our healthcare system works hard to manage.

question: Why must a hospital's internal policy always respect national nursing council regulations?

options.A: National councils pay for the printing of hospital rulebooks
options.B: It makes the hospital paperwork look neat and organized
options.C: Lower-level policies can never contradict higher regulatory frameworks
options.D: It allows nurses to ignore doctors' written prescriptions

explanation: In healthcare law, local rules must always align with and support higher national laws and professional board regulations.

question: Why do nurses flush an intermittent IV line with normal saline right after giving a medication?

options.A: To clear remaining drug residue and prevent line clotting
options.B: To dilute any air bubbles that entered during the injection
options.C: To numb the vein so the patient feels less soreness
options.D: To cool down the internal walls of the plastic tubing

explanation: Well done! Flushing pushes any leftover medication completely through the catheter, keeping the line clear and preventing clots.

question: Which of the following is a major barrier to safe motherhood in Nigeria?

options.A: An overabundance of fully equipped emergency hospitals
options.B: Too many skilled midwives working in remote villages
options.C: Free transportation services for all pregnant women
options.D: Inadequate health infrastructure and out-of-pocket spending

explanation: Poor facilities and the burden of paying out-of-pocket for treatment prevent many Nigerian women from getting timely care. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T44#GNS214_U1_T44_h8)

question: What term describes a resting adult heart rate that is consistently below 60 beats per minute?

options.A: Asystole
options.B: Tachycardia
options.C: Arrhythmia
options.D: Bradycardia

explanation: Bradycardia is the medical term for a slower-than-normal resting heart rate, defined in adults as under 60 beats per minute. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T8#GNS111_U2_T8_h5)

question: Why is good communication especially critical in busy primary health clinics?

options.A: It prevents dangerous mistakes caused by misunderstood instructions
options.B: It removes the need for doctors in the clinic
options.C: It allows the nurse to spend less time working with patients
options.D: It completely stops patients from seeking traditional healers

explanation: When clinics are crowded and resources are stretched, clear communication ensures patients still understand their medications and care instructions, avoiding serious errors. [learn more](GNS124_U5_T12#GNS124_U5_T12_h1)

question: How do deep, widespread fungal infections often show up in lung tissue scans?

options.A: As watery blisters covering the outer skin layer
options.B: As acute pus-filled abscesses with rapid cell rupture
options.C: As a gray pseudomembrane blocking the trachea
options.D: As granulomatous lesions that resemble tuberculosis

explanation: Fungi love to form granulomas in the lungs just like TB does, which can sometimes make them tricky to tell apart on an X-ray!

question: Why can it be dangerous to combine an expectorant with a cough suppressant?

options.A: It can trap thinned mucus in the airways if the patient cannot cough
options.B: It leads to severe kidney failure within twenty-four hours
options.C: It completely neutralizes the chemical structure of both drugs
options.D: It causes an immediate and dangerous drop in the patient's heart rate

explanation: Think about it: if the drug turns the mucus watery but you stop the patient from coughing, that fluid gets trapped and blocks their airway. Dangerous combo!

question: A patient has a thick scar right across their elbow joint. What problem can this cause over time?

options.A: Reduced range of motion in the arm
options.B: Complete loss of skin sensation
options.C: Permanent hair loss on the forearm
options.D: Spontaneous bleeding from the scar

explanation: Well done! Thick scars over joints act like tight rubber bands, making it hard to move that body part fully.

question: Which chemical messenger in the brain primarily acts to inhibit electrical activity and calm neurons down?

options.A: Sodium
options.B: Glutamate
options.C: GABA
options.D: Calcium

explanation: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter that helps prevent excessive electrical firing in the brain. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T16#GNS222_U3_T16_h2)

question: An audit shows nurses forget pain scores because the chart has no space for them. What is the best fix?

options.A: Suspending every nurse working on the ward without pay
options.B: Banning the use of all written documents on the hospital ward
options.C: Telling patients they must diagnose their own pain levels
options.D: Redesigning the pain chart to include a clear, dedicated space for scores

explanation: Smart thinking! Fixing the document layout makes proper charting much easier for busy nurses, solving the root cause of the missing data.

question: When checking a patient's walking stick (cane) or walker, what is the most important thing for you as a nurse to verify?

options.A: Instructing the patient to use it only during nighttime hours
options.B: Ensuring the device is the correct height and in good repair
options.C: Painting the frame a bright color so it looks modern
options.D: Replacing the assistive device with a wheelchair immediately

explanation: A worn-out or poorly adjusted walking aid can actually cause unsteadiness and lead to another fall. Always check the height and rubber tips!

question: What is the main problem when the heart suddenly fails to pump properly?

options.A: An immediate and permanent increase in body temperature
options.B: Complete paralysis of the skeletal muscles in the lower limbs
options.C: Uncontrolled overproduction of red blood cells in the bone marrow
options.D: A dangerous drop in systemic blood pressure and oxygen delivery

explanation: If the heart pump slows or stops, pressure drops and oxygen stops reaching the tissues that need it most. Spotting this early saves lives!

question: Why should nurses be involved when high-level health decisions are being made?

options.A: It allows nurses to manage hospital finances without auditing
options.B: It ensures policies reflect practical realities of patient care
options.C: It guarantees that doctors will no longer work in hospitals
options.D: It stops the government from spending money on medication

explanation: Spot on! When nurses have a seat at the table, the resulting rules make sense for everyday clinical work.

question: What severe long-term complication can happen when a baby's head presses against soft tissues for too long during obstructed labour?

options.A: Hyperemesis gravidarum
options.B: Pregnancy-induced hypertension
options.C: Obstetric fistula
options.D: Gestational diabetes

explanation: You nailed it. Prolonged pressure cuts off blood to the tissue between the bladder and vagina, which can cause an opening (fistula) to form. Prevention is key!

question: What is the best way for a nurse to find out how much pain a patient is feeling?

options.A: Asking the patient and listening to them
options.B: Looking at the size of the injury
options.C: Watching for changes in resting pulse
options.D: Checking lab results for inflammation

explanation: Pain is personal! Only the patient truly knows what they are feeling, so their word is always our best guide.

question: What is one of the primary frontline duties of a community health nurse during an outbreak?

options.A: Manufacturing vaccines in a laboratory setting
options.B: Managing international airport immigration desks
options.C: Tracing contacts and listing exposed individuals
options.D: Writing national health legislation and edicts

explanation: Community health nurses actively participate in contact tracing to identify and monitor those who need quarantine. [learn more](GNS313_U2_T5#GNS313_U2_T5_h9)

question: When talking about anticholinergic toxicity, what does the classic phrase 'dry as a bone' mean?

options.A: Extreme brittleness of the bones
options.B: Lack of calcium in the bloodstream
options.C: Loss of sweating and body secretions
options.D: Severe dehydration from diarrhea

explanation: Spot on! It means sweat, saliva, and mucus production completely shut down, leaving the skin and mouth very dry.

question: A shortage of which mineral leads to an enlarged thyroid gland, known as a goiter?

options.A: Iodine
options.B: Calcium
options.C: Iron
options.D: Zinc

explanation: You got it! Iodine helps the thyroid gland make important hormones. Without enough iodine, the thyroid swells up, causing a goiter. [learn more](GNS313_U3_T7#GNS313_U3_T7_h2)

question: What is the basic structural and functional unit of the human body?

options.A: A tissue
options.B: The molecule
options.C: The cell
options.D: An organ

explanation: The cell is universally recognized as the smallest independent unit that can carry out all life processes in the body. [learn more](GNS111_U1_T5#GNS111_U1_T5_h1)

question: An older adult lost their spouse recently and now seems very forgetful with medications. What is the most likely reason?

options.A: Intentional non-compliance with prescribed medication regimens
options.B: Cognitive overload and distress related to acute grief
options.C: An irreversible neurodegenerative condition like Alzheimer disease
options.D: An acute urinary tract infection causing sudden delirium

explanation: You're doing great! Acute grief can drain a person's mental energy and cause poor concentration. Always check for grief before jumping to conclusions like dementia!

question: Which of these is a common way nurses check a patient's nutritional status?

options.A: Listening to bowel sounds with a stethoscope for one hour
options.B: Testing daily urine output for trace mineral concentrations
options.C: Calculating Body Mass Index (BMI) and reviewing diet history
options.D: Measuring brain wave activity using specialized electrodes

explanation: As a nurse, checking physical measurements like BMI and asking about daily eating habits are quick, effective ways to spot nutritional issues.

question: What is the main goal when continuing education helps nurses drop old habits and adopt proven, modern methods?

options.A: Universal staffing
options.B: Preventing obsolescence
options.C: Mandatory licensing
options.D: Administrative control

explanation: Don't let the big word scare you—'preventing obsolescence' simply means making sure we don't use outdated or unsafe methods when science has found a better way!

question: What is the most important instruction for a patient going home with oral antibiotics for salpingitis?

options.A: Only treat your partner if they develop a fever
options.B: Resume sexual activity immediately if you feel fine
options.C: Stop taking the pills as soon as your belly pain stops
options.D: Finish all the medication even if you start feeling better

explanation: Always remind patients to finish their full course of antibiotics so the infection doesn't bounce back stronger!

question: When nurses interview local leaders and hold listening sessions during a community assessment, what kind of information are they gathering?

options.A: Qualitative insights
options.B: Quantitative statistics
options.C: Pharmacological logs
options.D: Genomic sequences

explanation: You've got this! Interviews and listening sessions give you qualitative data—meaning the real stories, lived experiences, and personal views of community members that numbers alone can't show.

question: What is a major reason why gifted children often feel lonely or isolated from others?

options.A: Difficulty finding peers who share their advanced interests
options.B: Mandatory isolation imposed by school policies
options.C: A total lack of interest in human relationships
options.D: Physical inability to leave the home environment

explanation: When your mind is working on complex topics, it can be tough to find kids your own age who want to talk about the same things. Makes total sense, right?

question: What do we mean when we say a bacterium has innate resistance?

options.A: It develops after a patient completes a full course of drugs
options.B: It is a natural, built-in characteristic of a bacterial species
options.C: It is acquired from other bacteria via horizontal gene transfer
options.D: It appears only when the patient has a weakened immune system

explanation: Innate means it was born that way! Some bacteria naturally have built-in defenses against certain drugs without ever needing prior exposure. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T92#GNS214_U1_T92_h3)

question: Which level of prevention uses routine immunizations to stop a disease before it even starts?

options.A: Tertiary prevention
options.B: Primary prevention
options.C: Primordial prevention
options.D: Secondary prevention

explanation: Spot on! Primary prevention is all about stopping health problems before they begin—vaccines are a classic example. Brilliant work!

question: How do RFID tags help clinical staff manage equipment?

options.A: By diagnosing equipment mechanical failures before they happen
options.B: By allowing rapid tracking and location of mobile medical devices
options.C: By cleaning and sterilizing surgical instruments automatically
options.D: By measuring the exact battery life of infusion pumps

explanation: RFID tags emit radio signals that let staff pinpoint the exact location of valuable mobile hospital equipment. [learn more](GNS113_U4_T5#GNS113_U4_T5_h2)

question: What special room feature do you need for a patient on Airborne Precautions?

options.A: Negative pressure airflow
options.B: An attached private sunroom
options.C: Open windows for natural breeze
options.D: Positive pressure ventilation

explanation: A negative pressure room pulls air in instead of blowing it out into the hallway when the door opens, trapping germs inside.

question: What is the main antiviral drug used to treat Lassa fever?

options.A: Chloroquine
options.B: Ribavirin
options.C: Artemether
options.D: Acyclovir

explanation: Ribavirin is the go-to antiviral. When given early, it drastically lowers the severity of the illness and saves lives.

question: A hospital wants shock-resistant drives for mobile nursing carts that load patient charts instantly. Which one should they pick?

options.A: Compact Disc (CD-ROM)
options.B: Hard Disk Drive (HDD)
options.C: Magnetic tape reel
options.D: Solid State Drive (SSD)

explanation: SSDs have no spinning parts, making them super tough for mobile carts rolling down hospital corridors and much faster than old-school hard drives!

question: What is the main role of contract management in healthcare outsourcing?

options.A: Designing architectural floor plans for new private hospital wings
options.B: Handling patient complaints regarding physician misdiagnoses
options.C: Managing nursing shift rosters and clinical staff promotions
options.D: Monitoring vendor performance and enforcing service-level agreements

explanation: Contract managers act like referees, making sure the private vendor actually delivers the quality of service they promised.

question: When you measure a patient's mid-upper arm circumference and body mass index, what kind of assessment are you doing?

options.A: Environmental factors
options.B: Biochemical data
options.C: Clinical signs
options.D: Anthropometric measurements

explanation: Don't let the big word scare you! 'Anthropometric' just means measuring physical body sizes like height, weight, and arm circumference to check nutrition.

question: Under which main category of health determinants does unemployment fall?

options.A: Social determinants
options.B: Microbiological agents
options.C: Genomic factors
options.D: Anatomical structures

explanation: Spot on! Unemployment directly affects daily living conditions and financial security, making it a major social determinant of health. You've got this! [learn more](GNS225_U5_T18#GNS225_U5_T18_h1)

question: What makes foetal hemoglobin different from adult hemoglobin?

options.A: It is produced exclusively in the placenta
options.B: It has a higher affinity for oxygen
options.C: It carries carbon dioxide instead of oxygen
options.D: It breaks down much faster in cold temperatures

explanation: Foetal hemoglobin grabs onto oxygen much more tightly, enabling the baby to extract oxygen from maternal blood. [learn more](GNS121_U6_T8#GNS121_U6_T8_h5)

question: As a nurse, what is a crucial check to make *before* a patient goes for a liver biopsy?

options.A: Check that clotting blood tests are safe and consent is signed
options.B: Perform a minor surgery to drain belly fluid
options.C: Give them strong general anesthesia right in the ward
options.D: Make sure they eat a large heavy meal

explanation: Spot on! Safety first—always verify clotting labs and make sure the patient understands and signs the consent form before the procedure.

question: What quick, easy test can you perform right at the bedside to check a patient's hearing?

options.A: Electroencephalogram
options.B: Computed tomography scan
options.C: Whispered voice test
options.D: Complete blood count

explanation: The whispered voice test is a fast, free, and easy bedside screening tool to check if a patient can hear soft sounds.

question: Why is it important to encourage a labouring mum to empty her bladder regularly?

options.A: To speed up cervical dilation past 10 centimeters
options.B: To stop Braxton Hicks contractions from returning
options.C: To prevent the bladder from obstructing fetal descent
options.D: To collect urine for a daily routine glucose test

explanation: Brilliant! A full bladder gets in the way like a water balloon in the pelvis, which can slow down the baby's journey down the birth canal.

question: What kind of healthcare service should form the solid base of a healthy community's health system?

options.A: Traditional herbal medicine centers exclusively
options.B: Private specialist clinics for high-income earners
options.C: Primary healthcare focused on prevention and promotion
options.D: Expensive tertiary care hospitals with advanced surgery

explanation: Primary care brings basic check-ups, vaccines, and health education right to the grassroots where people live.

question: When scientific research is described as 'empirical', what does that mean?

options.A: It is based on direct observation and real-world data
options.B: It focuses only on historical events from the past
options.C: It changes every time a new person reads the report
options.D: It relies entirely on the personal opinion of the researcher

explanation: Well done! Empirical simply means it is built on tangible evidence and real-world observations, not just guesses.

question: Why do we use the nursing diagnosis 'Fatigue' for someone with anemia?

options.A: To ensure the patient stays on strict bed rest all day
options.B: To prove the patient is not sleeping well at night
options.C: To address reduced oxygen-carrying capacity in the blood
options.D: To document that the patient is refusing hospital food

explanation: Anemia means fewer red blood cells to ferry oxygen around. Less oxygen means less energy for the body—hence, deep fatigue!

question: As a nurse, what is a major safety risk you must watch out for in patients with advanced Parkinson's disease?

options.A: Aspiration due to swallowing difficulties
options.B: Spontaneous regeneration of nerve tissue
options.C: Sudden permanent paralysis of the lower limbs
options.D: Excessive weight gain from hyperactive metabolism

explanation: Swallowing problems (dysphagia) are very common in late-stage Parkinson's. If food or saliva goes down the 'wrong pipe', it can lead to dangerous chest infections or choking.

question: Which of these directly makes the heart muscle demand more oxygen?

options.A: A decreased force of heart contraction
options.B: An increased heart rate
options.C: A lower blood pressure reading
options.D: Relaxation of the coronary arteries

explanation: When the heart beats faster, it pumps more and works harder, which means it burns through a lot more oxygen. Makes total sense when you picture it!

question: What is the main focus of 'staffing' in nursing management?

options.A: Creating policies for infection control
options.B: Designing the architectural layout of a new hospital building
options.C: Purchasing new lab equipment
options.D: Placing the right number of qualified nurses on the floor for every shift

explanation: Staffing is all about recruitment, scheduling, and making sure you have enough hands on deck.

question: A rescue team is about to free a trapped miner whose legs were under rubble for hours. What critical medical step must nurses prepare for?

options.A: Preparing the patient for immediate general anesthesia in the field
options.B: Withholding all fluids to prevent severe pulmonary edema
options.C: Applying a tight tourniquet to every limb before any movement starts
options.D: Administering large volumes of intravenous fluids to prevent kidney failure

explanation: Spot on! When trapped limbs are freed, toxins rush into the bloodstream. IV fluids help flush these out before they can shut down the kidneys.

question: Why should anti-diarrhea medications be used with extreme caution in food poisoning?

options.A: They stop IV fluids from working in the stomach
options.B: They can stop the body from pushing out harmful toxins and bacteria
options.C: They immediately trigger severe high blood pressure
options.D: They permanently damage the kidneys and liver

explanation: Makes sense, right? Sometimes diarrhea is the body's way of clearing out the bad stuff. Slowing it down too much can trap the germs inside. Great nursing insight!

question: What is the absolute go-to, life-saving medication for a patient experiencing dangerous anaphylaxis?

options.A: Epinephrine
options.B: Albuterol
options.C: Diphenhydramine
options.D: Hydrocortisone

explanation: Correct! Epinephrine acts fast to open closed airways and shoot blood pressure back up when seconds count in a severe allergic emergency.

question: What do we mean by 'nutrient quantification' in nursing and nutrition?

options.A: The process of measuring exact amounts of nutrients in food or the body
options.B: The chemical breakdown of proteins in the stomach
options.C: The calculation of total daily fluid intake and output
options.D: The surgical removal of excess fat tissue from the abdomen

explanation: Think of nutrient quantification as measuring out the exact amounts of nutrients someone eats or needs. You're doing great!

question: How are Dietary Reference Intakes (DRIs) usually used in everyday practice?

options.A: To treat acute vitamin toxicity in emergency rooms
options.B: To plan and evaluate nutrient intakes for healthy populations
options.C: To calculate exact medication dosages for surgical patients
options.D: To diagnose rare metabolic genetic diseases

explanation: DRIs give nurses and dietitians a helpful baseline to check if healthy groups are getting the right amount of nutrients.

question: How does an autoclave mainly manage to sterilize instruments?

options.A: Dry heat ovens operating at extreme electrical voltages
options.B: Saturated steam under pressure to denature proteins
options.C: Ultraviolet light rays penetrating bacterial cell walls
options.D: High-frequency ultrasonic waves to create microscopic bubbles

explanation: Think of an autoclave like a heavy-duty pressure cooker. The intense combination of steam and high pressure quickly destroys microbial proteins and kills all life forms.

question: How do unpredictable weather events directly impact food supply costs?

options.A: By destroying harvests, which reduces supply and drives up production expenses
options.B: By increasing the availability of cheap chemical fertilizers
options.C: By lowering the general cost of running heavy farm machinery
options.D: By stabilizing farmworker wages across different agricultural regions

explanation: Natural disasters and bad weather ruin crops, making available food scarcer and more expensive to produce. [learn more](GNS227_U2_T026#GNS227_U2_T026_h2)

question: A researcher creates a survey for anxiety, but the questions actually measure physical hunger. What is wrong with this tool?

options.A: Validity
options.B: Sample size
options.C: Secondary source status
options.D: Reliability

explanation: Validity is about whether your tool measures what it claims to measure. If it measures hunger instead of anxiety, its validity is off!

question: Why do nurse educators prefer active participation over just talking at you for an hour?

options.A: It improves knowledge retention and practical skill development
options.B: It allows the instructor to rest during the class session
options.C: It guarantees that students will never make clinical errors
options.D: It eliminates the need for any lesson planning

explanation: Doing and discussing makes your brain work harder than just listening, meaning you'll remember the steps way better on the ward!

question: A 16-year-old girl is afraid to ask her boyfriend to use a condom because he gets angry and threatens to leave. What does this situation show?

options.A: A minor disagreement regarding household chores and budget
options.B: Normal adolescent independence and healthy relationship bonding
options.C: A lack of basic anatomical knowledge about the reproductive system
options.D: Unequal power dynamics that compromise negotiation and safety

explanation: Spot on. Fear and threats in a relationship create a power imbalance, making it very hard for someone to protect their own health.

question: During the cardinal movements of labour, what happens during 'flexion'?

options.A: The fetal chin tucks against the chest
options.B: The widest part of the head enters the pelvis
options.C: The shoulders deliver from the birth canal
options.D: The fetal head rotates to face the spine

explanation: Think of a baby doing a little chin-tuck (flexion) so their head fits through the pelvis much easier. Smart little ones!

question: What is an important job for nurse managers who deal with financial data?

options.A: Approving pharmaceutical manufacturing licenses
options.B: Fixing broken hospital electrical wiring
options.C: Defending staffing levels and resource needs
options.D: Auditing national tax collection records

explanation: Having good cost data lets nurse managers confidently fight for enough staff and supplies to keep patients safe.

question: Why are run charts and graphs so commonly used in healthcare data analysis?

options.A: To replace patient medical records with colorful artwork
options.B: To hide negative patient statistics from regulatory inspectors
options.C: To calculate the daily nursing staff roster automatically
options.D: To help clinical teams easily visualize trends and patterns over time

explanation: Graphs make it super easy to look at numbers and instantly see if things are getting better or worse over weeks and months.

question: What is the main difference between a vaccine contraindication and a precaution?

options.A: A contraindication greatly increases the risk of a serious adverse reaction
options.B: A precaution means the vaccine will definitely cause immediate death
options.C: A contraindication only applies to adult travelers and never infants
options.D: A precaution requires doubling the standard pediatric vaccine dose

explanation: Contraindications mean the risk of harm clearly outweighs any potential benefit, making the vaccine unsafe to administer. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T73#GNS214_U1_T73_h3)
